source_text: Hujus memores pronuntiationis, tanquam praescriptionis, nihilominus quam stultum et impossibile sit aqua reformari tractamus. Quid utique ista materia tantae dignationis meruerit officium? Ut opinor, auctoritas liquidi elementi exigenda est. Atquin plurima suppetit, et quidem a primordio. Nam unum ex his est quae ante omnem mundi suggestum impolita adhuc specie penes Deum quiescebant: In primordio, inquit, fecit Deus coelum et terram. Terra autem erat invisibilis et incomposita, et tenebrae erant super abyssum, et spiritus Dei super aquas ferebatur. Habes, homo, imprimis aetatem venerari aquarum, quod antiqua substantia; dehinc dignationem, quod divini spiritus sedes, gratior scilicet caeteris tunc elementis. Nam et tenebrae totae adhuc sine cultu siderum informes, et tristis abyssus, et terra imparata, et coelum rude: solus liquor, semper materia perfecta, laeta simplex, de suo pura, dignum vectaculum Deo subjiciebat. Quid quod exinde dispositio mundi modulatricibus quodammodo aquis Deo constitit. Nam, ut firmamentum coeleste suspenderet, in medietate distinctis aquis fecit; et, ut terram aridam suspenderet, segregatis aquis expediit. Ordinato dehinc per elementa mundo cum incolae darentur, primis aquis praeceptum est animas proferre. Primus liquor quod viveret edidit ne mirum sit, in Baptismo, si aquae animare, noverunt. Nam ipsius quoque hominis figurandi opus, sociantibus aquis absolutum est. De terra materia convenit, non tamen habilis nisi humecta et succida, quam scilicet ante quartum diem segregatae aquae in stationem suam, superstite humore, limo temperarant. Si exinde universa vel plura prosequar quae de elementi istius auctoritate commemorem, quanta vis ejus aut gratia, quot ingenia, quot officia, quantum instrumentum mundo ferat; vereor ne laudes aquae potius, quam Baptismi rationes videar congregasse. Licet eo plenius docerem non esse dubitandum, si materiam, quam in omnibus rebus et operibus suis Deus disposuit, etiam in sacramentis propriis parere fecit; si quae vitam terrenam gubernat, et in coelesti procurat.
pass_a_gloss: Being mindful of this pronouncement, as if a prescription, we nonetheless treat how foolish and impossible it is for water to be reformed. What, indeed, has this material deserved such a great office? As I think, the authority of the liquid element must be exacted. And indeed, very much is supplied, and indeed from the beginning. For one of these is what, before every suggestion of the world, still unpolished in appearance, rested with God: In the beginning, it says, God made heaven and earth. But the earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was over the abyss, and the Spirit of God was borne over the waters. You have, man, first to venerate the age of the waters, because it is an ancient substance; then the dignity, because it is the seat of the divine Spirit, certainly more pleasing than the other elements at that time. For even the darkness, still entirely without the cultivation of the stars, unformed, and the gloomy abyss, and the unprepared earth, and the rough heaven: only the liquid, always a perfect material, joyful, simple, pure from its own, was presenting a worthy vehicle to God. What, indeed, from then on, the disposition of the world, in a certain way, was established by God with the moderating waters? For, in order that He might suspend the heavenly firmament, He made it in the middle, with the waters distinct; and, in order that He might suspend the dry earth, He prepared it with the waters separated. Then, with the world ordered through the elements, when inhabitants were given, the first waters were commanded to produce souls. The first liquid, because it lived, produced, so that it is not wonderful, in Baptism, if waters animate, they know. For the work of also forming man was completed, with the waters assisting. The material from the earth was suitable, but not, however, usable unless moist and succulent, which, certainly, before the fourth day, the separated waters, with the moisture remaining, had tempered into mud. If from then on I were to follow up all or most of the things that I might mention about the authority of this element, how great its power or grace, how many talents, how many offices, how much instrument it brings to the world; I fear lest I seem to have gathered praises of water rather than reasons for Baptism. Although I could teach more fully that it is not to be doubted, if the material, which God arranged in all things and works, He also made to serve in His own sacraments; if what governs earthly life also provides for heavenly life.

bible_refs.note: In the beginning God made heaven and earth

pass_b_english: Mindful of that pronouncement as if it were a prescription, we nonetheless argue how foolish and impossible it is for water to be reformed. What has this substance done to deserve so great an office? In my view, we must demand the authority of the liquid element, and indeed it supplies abundant evidence from the very beginning. One of the things that rested with God before any formation of the world, still unpolished in appearance, was this: In the beginning God made heaven and earth. But the earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness lay over the abyss, and the Spirit of God hovered over the waters (Genesis 1:1-2). So, first, you must venerate the antiquity of the waters because they are an ancient substance; then their dignity, because they served as the seat of the divine Spirit, making them certainly more pleasing than the other elements at that time. Even the darkness was still entirely unformed, lacking the adornment of the stars, and the gloomy abyss, the unprepared earth, and the rough heaven — only the liquid, always a perfect material, joyful, simple, pure of itself, presented a worthy vehicle to God. What is more, from then on the ordering of the world was established by God with the moderating waters. To suspend the heavenly firmament He made it in the middle with the waters divided; to suspend the dry land He prepared it with the waters separated. Later, when the world had been ordered through the elements and inhabitants were assigned, the first waters were commanded to produce living souls. The first liquid, because it was alive, produced life, so it should not be surprising that in Baptism waters know how to animate. Even the work of forming man was completed with the waters assisting. The material was taken from the earth, yet it was not usable unless moist and succulent, and the separated waters had tempered it into mud with their remaining moisture before the fourth day. If I went on to recount all or most of the things that attest the authority of this element — how great its power or grace, how many talents, offices, and services it renders the world — I fear I would seem to be gathering praises of water rather than reasons for Baptism. Yet I could teach more fully that there is no room for doubt: if God arranged this material in all things and works, He also made it serve in His own sacraments; if it governs earthly life, it also provides for heavenly life.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A preserves the clause structure and nuances (e.g., 'if waters animate, they know' for 'si aquae animare, noverunt'), while Pass B provides a fluent rendering that maintains the theological distinctions. Scripture citations (Genesis 1:1-2) are correctly applied to the quoted text.
